newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan goes to Washington to heal UN-USA wounds.
newsitem.headline: Annan goes to Washington to heal UN-USA wounds.

text.p: Barely in office, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who owes his job to the United States, was set to go to Washington to tell an array of officials how much they owed the world body he heads.

The trip, beginning on Wednesday afternoon, follows at least two years of relentless criticism of the United Nations, from conservatives contending the world body has too much power to radical militia imagining black U.N. helicopters swooping down on lawnchairs.

For Annan, the trip is a "time for healing," a veiled reference to the scorn heaped on the United Nations and his predecessor Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, driven from office by the Clinton administration at the end of a five-year term.
Annan, who headed U.N. peacekeeping, then became the favourite of Washington.

Soft-spoken, with considerable charm and frankness, the 58-year-old Ghanaian, who took office on Jan. 1, plans to make his case to leading senators and members of Congress that the United States needs the United Nations and vice versa. And this means paying the $1.3 billion debt owed by Washington that has crippled the world body.

"He has only a few months to cement the relationship and get the United States to really take its place among U.N. members and not shoot from the sidelines," said one senior official. "It is a healing time but not a long one."

U.S. President Bill Clinton proposed paying the debt by 1999, albeit with conditions. But whether the Republican-dominated Congress, which cut non-defence foreign aid to a bare minimlum, will agree was another question.
Annan on Thursday, was to see Clinton, U.S. Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright and National Security Council chief Sandy Berger, among others.

In attempting to shore up the U.N. relationship with Congress, Annan has scheduled meetings with a host of legislators including House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and North Carolina Sen. Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

But the wide gap between Democrats and Republicans was illustrated clearly in Helms' article in the Foreign Affairs magazine six months ago in which he advocated the United States withdraw from the United Nations unless its budget was slashed far more than anticipated so far.
Annan, since his election, has touted reform as a top priority and plans to come up with wide-ranging proposals in the next six months.

But he pointedly said reform did not mean massive or "arbitrary" cuts in vital programmes. Some nations, such as Japan, believed reform should not mean any lowering of dues, but release of funds for development to poor countries.

Since many of the bodies in the United Nations system were not under the control of the secretary-general but funded by voluntary contributions, Annan's influence on wide-ranging restructuring is often dependent on approval by member states.

But since the Clinton administration faulted Boutros-Ghali for allegedly not paying enough attention to reform, Annan was left with an albatross of massive change in order to get the United States to participate fully in the United Nations.
"It is up to the member states to define what they want the United Nations to be and to do -- to outline their vision of the goals they want us to attain and to set new priorities," he said.

Neverthless, the discussion of reform has brought up the question of a long-range purpose for the United Nations -- which many think rests on development strategies and assistance and peacemaking and peacekeeping.

But with money for poor states dwindling daily and nations such as the United States shy of undertaking major new peacekeeping missions, Annan has his work cut out for him in defining and getting others to agree on the United Nations' future.
